summary: A topological sort orders the vertices of a directed acyclic graph (DAG) so that every edge u -> v has u before v. It answers 'what order can I do things in, given prerequisites?', and exists only if the graph has no directed cycle.

sections.heading: Requirements
sections.body: Only DAGs have a topological order. A cycle makes the constraints contradictory (A before B before A), and undirected edges carry no direction. The order is usually not unique.

sections.heading: Kahn's algorithm (BFS)
sections.body: Compute every vertex's in-degree. Put all vertices with in-degree 0 in a queue. Repeatedly remove one, append it to the output, and decrement the in-degree of its neighbours, enqueueing those that reach 0. If the output has fewer than V vertices, the graph has a cycle.

sections.heading: DFS-based algorithm
sections.body: Run DFS; when a vertex finishes (all neighbours explored), push it on a stack. Popping the stack gives a topological order, because every vertex finishes after everything reachable from it.
sections.code:
dfs(u):
  visited[u] = true
  for v in adj[u]: if not visited[v]: dfs(v)
  push u onto stack      # finish time
# order = pop all of stack

sections.heading: Complexity
bullets: Space: O(V) for the queue/stack and in-degree or visited arrays.

sections.heading: Applications
bullets: Build systems: compile targets after their dependencies (make).
Task and job scheduling, spreadsheet cell evaluation order.
Dynamic programming over DAGs, such as longest path.

sections.body: Kahn: if fewer than V vertices were output, a cycle remains. DFS: if you reach a vertex that is currently on the recursion stack (a back edge), there is a cycle. Use three states: unvisited, in progress, done.

Edges: 5->2, 5->0, 4->0, 4->1, 2->3, 3->1. In-degrees: 0:2, 1:2, 2:1, 3:1, 4:0, 5:0. Queue starts with 4 and 5. Output 4 (frees nothing yet), 5 (frees 0 and 2), 0, 2 (frees 3), 3 (frees 1), 1: order 4 5 0 2 3 1.
Replace Kahn's FIFO queue with a priority queue so the smallest available vertex is always taken. This yields the lexicographically smallest topological order.
Process vertices in topological order, relaxing dist[v] = max(dist[v], dist[u] + w). Gives longest paths in O(V + E), unlike general graphs where longest path is NP-hard.
When cycles exist, compute SCCs (Tarjan or Kosaraju), contract each to a single node, and the result is a DAG you can topologically sort.

takeaways: Order vertices so every edge points forward; only possible for DAGs.
Kahn's BFS uses in-degrees; the DFS version reverses finish order.
O(V + E); detects cycles as a by-product.
Used for builds, scheduling, and DP on DAGs.
